title: 3.2 — Resilience & Reliability Patterns (Circuit Breaker, Saga, Bulkhead)

blocks.text: 3.2 — Resilience & Reliability Patterns (Circuit Breaker, Saga, Bulkhead)

items: Apply Circuit Breaker, Retry/Timeout, and Bulkhead to contain failures and protect availability.
Design Sagas for distributed transactions and choose between orchestration and choreography.
Use Rate Limiting and Fallback to keep systems stable under load and partial failure.
Reason about failure as a normal condition in distributed systems, not an exception.
Circuit Breaker — a proxy that stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold, failing fast during the open state and testing recovery.
Bulkhead — isolating resources (threads, connections, pools) so one overloaded component cannot exhaust shared capacity.
Retry / Timeout — bounded re-attempts with backoff; timeouts prevent indefinite waits.
Saga — a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions to achieve distributed consistency.
Orchestration (Saga) — a central coordinator drives each step and compensation.
Choreography (Saga) — services react to events; no central coordinator.
Rate Limiting — capping request rate to protect a service from overload.
Fallback — a degraded but safe response when a dependency fails (cache, default, stub).

blocks.text: In distributed systems, partial failure is the steady state: a dependency will be slow or dead. The goal is to contain failure so one broken component degrades gracefully instead of cascading into a full outage. This is the job of resilience patterns.

items: Timeout: never wait forever. Bound every remote call; release the thread.
Retry with backoff + jitter: transient errors (network blips) often succeed on retry, but naive retries can amplify load — use exponential backoff and jitter, and only retry idempotent operations.

Circuit Breaker: wraps a call and tracks failures. After a threshold, it "opens" and fails fast without making the call, giving the dependency time to recover; after a cool-down it lets a trial call through (half-open). This prevents hammering a struggling service.
Bulkhead: partition resources (e.g., separate thread pools per downstream). If the payment pool is exhausted, the shipping path still works. Like compartments in a ship, one flood doesn't sink all.

blocks.text: A single ACID transaction cannot span microservices (they own their databases). A Saga replaces the distributed transaction with a sequence of local transactions; each step has a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: Create Order → Reserve Inventory → Charge Card; if charging fails, compensate by releasing inventory and cancelling the order.

Orchestration uses a central coordinator (e.g., a Saga orchestrator/state machine) that tells each service what to do and triggers compensations. It is easier to reason about and debug, but adds a central component. Choreography has services react to each other's events with no coordinator; it is more decoupled and resilient to central failure, but harder to trace and easy to tangle. Choose orchestration for complex, critical flows (clear blame, easy monitoring) and choreography for simpler, loosely-coupled reactions.

Rate limiting (token bucket, leaky bucket) protects a service from spikes and abusive clients, often at the gateway. Fallback provides a safe degraded path: return a cached catalog when the recommendation service is down, or a default shipping estimate. Together they keep the system "mostly working" rather than "hard down."

    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Open: failures >= threshold
    Open --> HalfOpen: after cool-down
    HalfOpen --> Closed: trial call OK
    HalfOpen --> Open: trial call fails

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant I as Inventory
    participant P as Payment
    O->>I: Reserve(id)
    I-->>O: reserved
    O->>P: Charge(id)
    alt charge fails
        P-->>O: error
        O->>I: Compensate: Release(id)
    else success
        P-->>O: ok
        O-->>O: Saga complete
    end
